title: Making Startups Powerful
gist: An essay arguing that the highest-leverage question for an early-stage company is not 'how can it make more money' but 'how can it become more powerful' — via owning the customer relationship, routing money (or AI tokens) through itself, manufacturing network effects, going full stack, giving away value, and acquiring customers and data as early upstream as possible. It claims these structural moves produce 10x-100x outcomes rather than incremental ones, and that they only work when they genuinely improve the customer's life.

themes.theme: Power vs. revenue as the optimizing question

insights.claim: Asking how a young company could become more powerful produces order-of-magnitude increases in value, whereas asking how it could make more money tends to yield only incremental improvements.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Screen portfolio companies on structural power moves (ownership of the customer, money flow, network effects) rather than near-term revenue optimization; the latter rarely changes the outcome distribution.
insights.quote: Asking how the company could make more money is a good heuristic too, but it tends to yield incremental improvements. Whereas thinking about how to make it more powerful will sometimes make it orders of magnitude more valuable.
insights.locator: One of the most useful heuristics I have

insights.claim: A reliable idea-generation heuristic is to ask in what ways a company's current idea is being held back by other companies, because most power strategies are really ways of escaping constraints imposed by suppliers, platforms or bureaucratic buyers.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: In diligence, map who structurally constrains the company; the size of the escape path is often the size of the upside.
insights.quote: In what ways is the current idea being held back by other companies?
insights.locator: Often what you're doing when you explore ways

insights.claim: Every power strategy is bounded by a hard constraint: it only works if the result is genuinely better for the customer, otherwise there is no uptake.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Treat structural land-grabs that degrade customer experience (forced bundling, artificial lock-in) as a red flag rather than a moat.
insights.quote: You can only do these things when the result is better for the customer. Otherwise you won't have any uptake.
insights.locator: But all these strategies for making startups more powerful

insights.claim: The constraint that a weak company can only grow by improving customers' lives can be run backwards as an idea generator: describe the perfect world from the customer's point of view, then see which component of it the company could become.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A cheap generative exercise for founders and investors sourcing new theses in a crowded category.
insights.quote: What would the perfect world look like, from the customer's point of view?
insights.locator: These are strategies for making startups powerful in the long term

insights.claim: Newly founded startups are good for the world precisely because they are too weak to force anything on anyone, so their only path to power runs through making customers better off.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A defense of early-stage venture as socially productive; also implies the customer-alignment dividend erodes once a company becomes powerful.
insights.quote: Newly founded startups are too weak to force anything on anyone.
insights.locator: These are strategies for making startups powerful in the long term

themes.theme: Owning the relationship and routing money (and tokens) through you

insights.claim: Transforming a company from a mere component supplier into the party that owns the customer relationship, and making money flow through it, is one of the highest-value structural changes available.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Valuation multiples should reward the layer that owns the end customer and the payment rail, not the layer that ships parts into someone else's box.
insights.quote: It's always good when money flows through you.
insights.locator: Is there a way to transform the company

insights.claim: In AI, making tokens flow through you usually means money flows through you too, putting you in the customer-owning position while model providers become component suppliers — but the open question is how easily those model companies could engulf you or your customers.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: The central bull/bear question for the AI application layer: token intermediaries capture the relationship, but face forward-integration risk from the foundation model labs.
insights.quote: You own the customer relationship, and the model companies are in effect component suppliers. The question is how easy it would be for them to engulf you, or even your customers.
insights.locator: Notes [1] You can also make tokens flow through you

insights.claim: Going full stack — using your own technology to do x in competition with the companies you were selling it to — lets a company absorb what had been its customer and take over the outside surface of the market.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Watch for tools vendors quietly turning into operators; that transition is where multiple expansion and TAM redefinition happen.
insights.quote: instead of selling your technology to companies doing x, you use the technology yourself to do x in competition with them
insights.locator: There are certain kinds of thinking where ideas start to seem almost physical

insights.claim: A softer variant of going full stack is to eat gradually through the customer by taking over all their hardest work, until in the limit the company does all the brainwork and the original customer is reduced to running errands — effectively a hand puppet whose customer is now yours.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Particularly relevant for AI services businesses: the incremental takeover of cognitive work converts a vendor into the de facto principal, with the end customer's economics attached.
insights.quote: In the limit case, you're doing all the brainwork and they're just running errands for you.
insights.locator: There's a variant of going full stack

insights.claim: Moving upstream is almost always advantageous, whether upstream means money, the user relationship, the stage at which you acquire a customer, or data.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A single compact test for evaluating positioning across very different business models.
insights.quote: Upstream is almost always good, whether it's with money or user relationship or customer stage or data.
insights.locator: Upstream is almost always good

insights.claim: Network effects can often be deliberately induced in products that would not naturally have them, and doing so sometimes converts a service into a marketplace and transforms the idea entirely.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Ask every service-business founder for the marketplace conversion path; the re-rating from service multiple to marketplace multiple is the prize.
insights.quote: It's surprising how often it can be done. And when it can, this sometimes transforms the idea completely; what had been a service is now a marketplace.
insights.locator: Network effects make companies more powerful

insights.claim: The AI-native way to induce network effects is to let users opt into training the model on their own interactions, so that the shared model outperforms the vanilla one used by those who decline.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Opt-in data flywheels create a visible performance gap between participants and holdouts — a concrete, measurable moat to test in AI product diligence.
insights.quote: The obvious AI variant is to let your users opt in to training your model on their interactions with it. Many will resist that, but if some don't, the model they get to use will outperform the vanilla one used by the others.
insights.locator: The deluxe version is full app store

insights.claim: A startup building payment rails for AI agents should first ask whether the agents can also pay one another, because that converts it into a marketplace — a prize valuable enough to justify reorienting the whole company and even acting as market maker to bootstrap liquidity.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A specific, timely test for the agentic-payments category now being funded: agent-to-agent settlement, not agent-to-merchant checkout, is where the durable value sits.
insights.quote: if I were talking to a startup building a way for agents to pay for things, the first question I'd ask is whether the agents could also pay one another
insights.locator: Often you can induce network effects by generalizing the idea

insights.claim: Building something like an app store means other companies' efforts to create value also increase your value, and it works best when combined with owning the customer relationship and routing the money.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Platform economics compound third-party R&D into your own asset base; look for the combination of ecosystem plus payment ownership.
insights.locator: Is there a way to create something akin to an app store

insights.claim: In a new field with no established standard, being early is enough to define it, because everyone is hungry for standards and the first proposal tends to win regardless of who proposed it.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: In emerging categories, small companies should aggressively publish interop standards early; standard authorship is an underpriced form of control.
insights.quote: everyone is so hungry for standards that the first to be proposed tends to win, no matter who proposed it
insights.locator: Notes [2] If you can't create an app store

insights.claim: Y Combinator itself is described as an accidental instance of network effects appearing in something nobody expected to have them, recognized only after it had already happened.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Evidence that network effects can emerge in non-obvious categories, supporting the search for them outside classic marketplace businesses.
insights.quote: We didn't intend it to be, but we realized very quickly that that was what we'd stumbled upon.
insights.locator: Notes [3] YC itself is an instance of network effects

themes.theme: Generosity, open source and API extensibility as power

insights.claim: Squeezing every last penny out of customers yields at most 2x returns, while discovering some new thing to make for them can yield 10x or 100x — so creating more value than you capture is the route to becoming really rich rather than idealistic sentiment.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Companies in aggressive monetization mode are usually signaling they have run out of new products; that shift is a late-cycle marker for an asset.
insights.quote: Squeezing every last penny out of customers is a distraction. It gets you 2x returns at most. Whereas discovering some new thing you could make for them could easily get you 10x or 100x returns.
insights.locator: Being generous makes you more powerful

insights.claim: When a company switches from making new products to squeezing more profit out of existing ones, it is often because control has passed from founders to hired managers, who take the company's power for granted rather than remembering when it had to delight users to survive.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Founder departure is a leading indicator of a shift from value creation to value extraction — a governance signal with direct implications for long-horizon holdings.
insights.quote: When companies switch from making new products to squeezing more profit out of existing ones, it's often because control has passed from the founders to hired managers.
insights.locator: Notes [5] The O'Reilly way of looking at the world

insights.claim: Open sourcing software is the classic case of generosity converting into power: giving the product away makes it a standard and makes users trust it, so it spreads and the company ends up with a small piece of a much larger pie.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Value open-source-led companies on category size captured rather than on license revenue given away.
insights.quote: They literally give away the product, but by giving it away they both make it a standard and make users trust it more.
insights.locator: The classic example of generosity leading to power

insights.claim: Letting your product be called via an API is the ultimate form of extensibility, and companies that refuse because they dislike the loss of control are usually making a mistake — especially now that agents rather than humans are becoming the users and nobody knows what they will want to do.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: API openness becomes a competitive variable as agent traffic grows; closed, UI-only products risk being routed around by agentic demand.
insights.quote: Especially now that agents are replacing human users. Who knows what they'll want to do? So err on the side of having APIs.
insights.locator: The ultimate in extensibility

insights.claim: Flexibility about extensibility may be the key to finally displacing Apple, because Apple can be relied upon to stay restrictive about hardware and software that integrates with its own.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: An explicit competitive attack vector on Apple: openness at the integration layer, not better hardware.
insights.quote: Perhaps flexibility in this department will be the key to finally displacing Apple.
insights.locator: Notes [6] Perhaps flexibility in this department

insights.claim: Selling at a loss can be worthwhile, but giving away too much destroys the signal customers send by paying, and a growth rate produced by selling a $10 bill for $5 tells you nothing useful.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Discount growth metrics from heavily subsidized products; the growth curve is not evidence of demand at a real price.
insights.quote: If your product is a $10 bill that you sell for $5, your growth rate isn't telling you anything useful.
insights.locator: Notes [4] There are even times when it's worthwhile to sell at a loss

themes.theme: Customer selection: early-stage buyers, fast deciders, and data upstream

insights.claim: Selling to earlier-stage companies makes a vendor more powerful despite those customers having less money, because usage-based revenue from them then grows at startup rates.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Net revenue retention from a young-company cohort on usage pricing can beat enterprise ACVs; look at customer trajectory, not current customer size.
insights.quote: Strangely enough, selling to earlier stage companies makes you more powerful.
insights.locator: Strangely enough, selling to earlier stage companies

insights.claim: Stripe deliberately signs up companies at the first possible moment because payments infrastructure is never replaced once working, so those customers effectively never churn.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A named template for infrastructure businesses: the combination of zero churn plus customer growth compounds without incremental sales cost.
insights.quote: With payments infrastructure, if it ain't broke, you don't fix it, and since Stripe ain't broke, companies that install it never churn.
insights.locator: This is why Stripe makes a point of signing up companies

insights.claim: A product that cannot be sold to a company until it has 500 people forces enterprise sales, which takes forever and is notoriously not a domain where the best product wins.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: High minimum-customer-size thresholds are a structural weakness, not a sign of an attractive ACV; ask whether the product can be tweaked to sell earlier.
insights.quote: Now you're doing enterprise sales, which takes forever and is notoriously not a domain where the best product wins.
insights.locator: Whereas if you're making something you can't sell

insights.claim: Customers who decide fast are valuable beyond the speed itself, because fast deciders decide based on quality, which routes the best product straight to the most money — whereas selling to hospitals and school districts is like walking through mud.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Decision speed of the buyer is a proxy for whether product quality converts into revenue; slow-buyer sectors systematically reward incumbency over merit.
insights.quote: customers who decide fast tend to decide based on how good you are
insights.locator: More generally, having customers who decide fast

insights.claim: Reframing the question from 'what size customers should we target' to 'at what point in their life should we acquire customers' reveals that targeting bigger companies is merely targeting a given company later, which is why growth rate matters more than absolute numbers.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Reprices the apparent trade-off between SMB and enterprise GTM: in decades-long thinking, customers have trajectories rather than fixed sizes.
insights.quote: If you think in quarters, it seems like potential customers have fixed sizes. If you think in decades, you can see they have trajectories.
insights.locator: Notes [7] If you switch from asking

insights.claim: Rippling deliberately started with onboarding software because that is where the life of employee data begins, using early data capture to become the operating system for employee-data applications and to run most of those applications itself.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A repeatable pattern: enter at the point of data origination and overbuild that wedge, because the wedge market is not the real prize.
insights.quote: since there was more at stake for them than just the onboarding software market, their onboarding software was way better than it needed to be, and spread rapidly
insights.locator: There's a strategy similar to getting the customers early

themes.theme: Tails wagging dogs and reading user misuse

insights.claim: PayPal began as security software for hand-held devices and the payments product was built merely as a demo, until eBay sellers adopted it and the founders conceded within a couple of months that this was now their business.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Justifies a standing question in every board meeting: could the peripheral feature be the real product? Pivot recognition speed is itself an investable trait.
insights.quote: They created Paypal as a demo of their security software. But then eBay sellers started using it to take payments
insights.locator: Another thing I'm always looking for is tails

insights.claim: Users 'misusing' a product to do something unintended signals demand so desperate that they will use things that are not even meant to be solutions, and that signal is more valuable than the annoyance it causes.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Off-label usage data is an early, cheap indicator of an adjacent market worth far more than the shipped product.
insights.quote: don't be annoyed that your users are using your product wrong; listen for the message they're sending, because it could be valuable
insights.locator: It's exciting when you notice users

insights.claim: PayPal grew fast because it helped users make money, and products that help users make money are both adopted quickly and paid a lot for, so revenues grow doubly fast — a property shared by most of the most successful YC-funded companies and by YC itself.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Prioritize products positioned on the customer's revenue line over those on the cost line; adoption speed and pricing power compound together.
insights.quote: When you help users make money, they're (a) quick to adopt your product and (b) will pay a lot for it. So your revenues grow doubly fast.
insights.locator: The reason Paypal grew so fast

themes.theme: Time horizon arbitrage and mafia markets

insights.claim: Trade-offs that only pay off in ten years are usually underpriced, because competing startups are run by opportunists hoping to be acquired and large counterparties are run by executives who expect to leave within a few years and think only about the current quarter.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A structural arbitrage available to patient capital: long-dated structural moves face systematically weak competition for them.
insights.quote: Most big companies you deal with will be run by executives who don't expect to be there for more than a few years and are only thinking about this quarter's numbers.
insights.locator: Playing the long game makes you more powerful

insights.claim: The recommended early pricing posture is to sell as cheaply as necessary to acquire all the users first and worry about margins later, though deeper structural ways to play the long game usually exist too.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Early gross margin compression can be a deliberate land-grab rather than a broken model; judge it against user acquisition velocity.
insights.quote: get all the users, then worry about your margins
insights.locator: Playing the long game makes you more powerful

insights.claim: Startups are strongest on level playing fields and weakest in mafia-like markets such as record labels and pharmacy benefit managers, where the best product does not win and a company may exist only for as long as the incumbents allow.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Two named sectors flagged as structurally hostile to new entrants; discount disruption theses aimed frontally at them.
insights.quote: Record labels are mafia. PBMs are mafia. In these worlds you don't win by having the best product.
insights.locator: Since startups make the best stuff

insights.claim: Mafia-like incumbents can probably be defeated only from the side — by making them irrelevant through winning in another dimension — rather than by frontal attack, so their defeat becomes an ancillary benefit rather than a prerequisite for success.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Favor flanking strategies in gatekept industries; a business plan whose success requires beating the gatekeeper head-on carries dependency risk.
insights.quote: you'd have to do it by coming in from the side — by somehow making them irrelevant, rather than by frontal attack
insights.locator: Since startups make the best stuff

insights.claim: A practical way to recognize mafia-style industries is that they are full of lawyers, a trait shared by record labels and pharmacy benefit managers.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: A crude but usable screen for sectors where legal leverage, not product quality, determines outcomes.
insights.quote: Apparently one thing record labels and PBMs have in common is that they're full of lawyers.
insights.locator: Notes [9] Apparently one thing record labels

insights.claim: In normal industries, customers slow to adopt new technology are an opportunity because the slower they are, the more likely a company can win by going full stack — but hospitals and school districts are grim precisely because that route is generally unavailable, though serving students directly can bypass schools.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Distinguishes exploitable laggards from unexploitable ones; in education the viable wedge named is direct-to-student rather than institutional sales.
insights.quote: there are some opportunities to go around schools and go directly to serving students
insights.locator: Notes [8] In a normal industry

insights.claim: A surprising share of startup advice contains the word 'just' — you don't need to do x, just do y — because ideas get twisted into knots by evolving from something else and carrying a part that is no longer needed.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Vestigial product complexity from a prior pivot is a common, cheaply fixable drag on early companies.
insights.quote: A surprising percentage of the advice I give to startups has the word "just" in it.
insights.locator: Often as not, though, startups are being held back by themselves

insights.claim: In very early stage companies, complicated ideas are often the product of fear — the company unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than it could — so the fix is less a strategy change than standing up straight.
insights.speaker: Paul Graham Essays
insights.so_what: Ambition deficits show up as complexity; probing for the scared-down version of the plan can surface a materially larger business.
insights.quote: The company is unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could.
insights.locator: Often as not, though, startups are being held back by themselves
